fatal_errors: The proposed refractory nanocrystalline BCC/Laves alloy is unrelated to the target as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 L12/B2 lamellar eutectic alloy.
The intervention omits the three-cycle 1100 °C thermal-shock treatment and replaces the target deionized-water tribocorrosion test with an unspecified abrasion test in sulfuric acid.
The baseline is a hypothetical coarse-grained version of the same alloy rather than identically conditioned duplex stainless steel 2205.

Neither cited source demonstrates simultaneous tribocorrosion, self-healing film kinetics, or the claimed causal role of nanocrystalline grain boundaries; E1 reports separate wear and electrochemical corrosion results, while E2 is principally a processing comparison.
explanation: The response addresses the broad wear-corrosion problem and captures one genuine part of the target mechanism: sliding removes a passive layer, while rapid repassivation can reduce friction, corrosion, and total damage. Its boundary that failure occurs when removal outpaces film repair is also scientifically reasonable. However, it does not reconstruct the material, thermal conditioning, comparator, aqueous conditions, temperature/load/frequency matrix, or the key non-monotonic temperature response. It misses the transition from abrasion at 25 °C to minimum-wear polishing near 50 °C and unstable oxidative or third-body wear at 100 °C, as well as the contrast between retained L12/B2 phase fractions in the HEA and major gamma-to-delta redistribution in DS2205. The proposed experiment could test a generic grain-size/passivation hypothesis, but processing coarse and nanocrystalline samples may also change phase constitution and chemistry, and the listed measurements do not directly establish film repair kinetics or decompose simultaneous wear and corrosion contributions. Most importantly, the supplied evidence does not substantiate the specific nanocrystalline grain-boundary/self-healing mechanism, so this is not a well-supported alternative to the target hypothesis.
